key_insight: Guideline-grounded claim verification reduced hallucinated content by an order of magnitude, but verifier reliability remained the main bottleneck.
clinical_relevance: For cardiology QA tools, automated verification can reduce errors but should not be treated as proof that an answer is clinically correct.
method: Built 160 internist-approved questions across four ESC cardiology guidelines and 627 hand-verified retrieval records.
Tested a five-stage verify-and-revise pipeline across four retrieval configurations and three independent runs.
Manually audited 606 flagged claims, independently re-judged 906 decisions, and blindly expert-reviewed 100 accepted claims.
evidence_signal: Only 44.7–50.6% of flagged claims were genuine hallucinations; final genuine errors affected 1.7% of answers, with 35% of genuine final errors introduced by correction.
watch_item: Evidence is limited to this guideline-grounded benchmark; single-run hallucination recall was only 35.6–41.2%, so automated acceptance can still miss errors.
paper_title: Mitigating Hallucinations in Medical Question Answering on ESC Cardiology Guidelines: Evaluation and Retrieval Optimization
